newsitem.title: USA: N. Plains, Midwest rail movement slowed by snow.
newsitem.headline: N. Plains, Midwest rail movement slowed by snow.

text.p: Heavy snow, ice and sub-zero temperatures in the upper U.S. Midwest and Northern Plains continued to hamper railroad movement Wednesday, railroad officials and grain dealers said.
"It's a blizzard up here," said one wheat dealer based in Minneapolis, Minn. "Nothing is moving at all."
Despite the harsh weather, a spokesman for Burlington Northern Santa Fe Corp said most of its main rail lines were now cleared.
The company on Wednesday was clearing smaller branch lines of snow in an area that spans much of the northern U.S.
"The territory from the Pacific Northwest across the northern tier of the Midwest was pretty hard hit," said Mike Martin, with Burlington Northern in Fort Worth, Texas.
"It took a number of days to plow out the main lines and now we're working on the branch lines," he said.

A spokesman for Union Pacific Corp in Omaha, Neb., which serves Minnesota, Wisconsin, Iowa and Nebraska, reported no tracks were shut down because of ice or snow, but trains were running slower because of the extreme cold.
"The cold weather causes some slowdown in operations because you can't run as fast when the weather gets down in the subzero cold temperatures," said Ed Trandahl, spokesman for Union Pacific.
Extreme cold causes icing on switches, additional stress on tracks and engines, and all those factors mean that trains will have to move more slowly, Trandahl said.

Grain dealers have reported that many farmers are unable to get their grain to elevators to sell, and some elevators are not receiving rail service. As a result, spring wheat cash values are climbing, dealers said.
Rail service and other traffic is not expected to return to normal until temperatures warm and the snow stops falling, but forecasters show more harsh weather on the way.

Temperatures in North Dakota were seen dropping to a low of minus 20 degrees Fahrenheit on Friday, while low temperatures in Minnesota were seen ranging from minus 17 to minus four degrees, according to data from Omaha-based forecasters, Weather Express Inc.
